setup.zh: 舅舅送你走了三天；天亮前，你把最后半张饼分给了牛棚里的孙二狗。三百级石阶直通云雾，顶上站着一个扫地的老头：「不看出身，不看荐书——只看三样：腿，脑子，胆子。」一试，腿：三百级，一炷香。
setup.en: Your uncle walked you three days; before dawn you gave the last half flatbread to Sun Ergou in the cowshed. Three hundred stone steps climb into the clouds, and at the top stands an old sweeper: "Not by birth, not by letters of recommendation — by three things only: legs, head, nerve." First trial, legs: three hundred steps, one stick of incense.

recap.zh: 一试，三百级石阶：你三步一吸，三步一呼，替舅舅走了上来。
recap.en: First trial, three hundred steps: three steps a breath in, three a breath out, you climbed the stair for your uncle.

zh: 石阶顶上，一个扫地的老头。
en: Three hundred steps, straight into the clouds.
At the top, an old man with a broom.
First trial, legs: one stick of incense.

story.zh:
九月初九，是重阳。照老例，这一天人人都要登高，插茱萸，喝菊花酒，说是登得越高，灾祸便躲得越远。这一年泗水边上的重阳，却登得与往年大不相同：几千个孩子，登的是同一座山，登的是同一道石阶，求的也不是躲灾，是求仙。

沉鼎观三年开一回山门，一回几千个孩子来爬这道石阶，收下的，不过百来个。三百年下来，约莫一百回，进过这道山门的，统共一万来人。这一万来人里，后来有练到练气九层的，有一辈子停在三四层、下山去做了郎中镖师的，有死在秘境里、连尸首也没找回来的；真正筑了基、踏进那道门槛的，三百年间，数来数去，不过百十个人。

从蒙山到泗水，要走三天。头一天走的是山路，小满背着爷爷那张弓，怀里揣着他娘给的针线、空钱袋和空本子，胸口还挂着一块谁也瞧不见的木牌，一路上不怎么说话。舅舅却说了一路。他讲他当年上沉鼎山，讲那三百级石阶是怎么一级一级长在云里的，讲他爬到一百六十级的时候，两条腿是怎么变成两根别人家的腿的。讲到傍晚歇脚，已讲了七遍。讲到第三遍，添了一段：他在一百二十级上看见一条蛇。讲到第五遍，那条蛇有胳膊粗了。讲到第七遍，那蛇朝他吐了吐信子，他瞪了它一眼，蛇便走了。小满听着，心想：这条蛇，大约也是每年都在长的。

那一夜，山脚下的客栈早住满了，连柴房都住满了，庙里的廊檐底下也躺满了人，舅舅花了十个铜钱，才在一户人家的牛棚里赁到半张草铺。牛棚里除了他们，还有一头牛，一家从兖州来的父子，和一个一声不吭的瘦孩子。那头牛嚼了一夜的草，兖州那个爹打了一夜的鼾，瘦孩子睁着眼睛看了一夜的房梁。那孩子十四五岁年纪，瘦得像一根晾衣竿，背着一个比他身子还大的包袱，包袱里鼓鼓囊囊，也不知装的什么。小满跟他搭话，问他叫什么，从哪来，他只说了两个字：「孙家。」再问，便不说了。半夜里，小满听见他在草铺上翻来覆去，嘴里小声念叨着什么，凑近了一听，念的是：「三步一口气，三步一口气……」原来他白天在河边，也听见了舅舅讲故事。小满也没怎么睡，他把胸口的木牌掏出来，捏在手心里。

天快亮的时候，小满从包袱里摸出一张饼来。四张饼，一路上舅舅讲故事，讲饿了三张，只剩了一张。他掰下一半，塞进嘴里，嚼着嚼着，看见草铺那头，那个叫孙家的瘦孩子也醒了，正盯着他手里那半张饼，喉头一动一动的。

小满看了看那半张饼，又看了看那孩子。

他想起谷底那一夜，想起那只断了尾巴的小狐狸，想起他掰给它的那一半鸡蛋、那一半饼。他那时候想的是：它饿。

他把手里那半张饼递了过去，道：「吃吧。今天要爬三百级呢。」

那孩子愣了一愣，接过去，一口塞进嘴里，嚼得很快，嚼完了，才想起来说：「……谢谢。」小满摆摆手。那孩子又道：「我叫孙二狗。」小满道：「沈小满。」孙二狗道：「我记着了。」

山门底下，另有一片空地，给人用绳子圈了起来，绳子里头站着十几个穿灰袍的执事，一个一个查验孩子的年纪、籍贯，又收兵刃。凡是带着刀剑弓棍的，一律要解下来，交给执事，拿一根竹签子记了名字，挂在一面木架上。执事说：「三试考的是人，不是家伙。」

小满便把爷爷那张弓解了下来。那弓在木架上挂着，夹在一排亮闪闪的刀剑中间，弓背上一道一道缠着牛筋，远远瞧过去，活像一条打了补丁的裤子，混在一群新衣裳里。旁边一个穿绸衫的孩子指着它，跟他爹笑得前仰后合。小满没理会，只把竹签子上自己的名字多看了两眼，记住了那弓挂在第三排左数第七个。

来的是一顶滑竿。四个轿夫抬着，两个家丁跟着，一个给马小宝打伞，一个给他扇扇子——这一天既没下雨，也没出太阳。马小宝坐在滑竿上，比去年又胖了一圈，手里捏着一块桂花糕，嘴里还嚼着一块，腮帮子一鼓一鼓的。他这一路从蒙山来，桂花糕是论斤带的，据说装了满满两个食盒，到了泗水已吃掉了一个半。马小宝一眼瞧见了小满，把嘴里那块咽下去，冲他扬了扬下巴，道：「哟，沈小满，你也来了？你们家那扇门，扛回来没有？」

小满道：「扛回来了，小宝哥。装得有点歪。」

辰时正，山门上「当」的一声，敲了一下钟。

几千个孩子霎时间静了下来。石阶顶上，不知什么时候站了一个扫地的老头，一身灰布短褂，拄着一把竹扫帚，佝偻着背，看都不看底下这几千个孩子一眼，只顾低着头，一下一下地扫他脚底下那一级台阶。那级台阶早给他扫得干干净净，亮得能照见人影，他还是扫。观里的老弟子说，这老头扫的，永远是这一级，第三百级，扫了五十年了。旁的台阶落了叶子、积了雪，他一概不管，只扫这一级。有人问他为什么，他说：「这一级，是人上来头一脚踩的。」再问，便不说了。

扫了好一会儿，他才开口，声音不高，却一个字一个字清清楚楚地落到山脚下来：「沉鼎观收人。不看出身，不看荐书——」

人群里「嗡」的一声。马小宝的脸白了一下。

那老头接着道：「——只看三样。腿。脑子。胆子。」

**一试 · 腿。**

三百级石阶，一炷香。

那扫地老头话音刚落，山门边的执事便点着了一炷香，插在一只铜炉里，喊了一声「开始」。这「开始」两个字还没落地，几千个孩子便一窝蜂地往上冲，冲得石阶上尘土飞扬，你推我搡，喊爹的、喊娘的、踩了别人鞋的、给别人踩了鞋的，乱成一锅粥，活像一群给人打开了笼门的鸭子。
story.en:
The ninth of the ninth month is Double Ninth. By old custom everyone climbs high that day, wears dogwood, drinks chrysanthemum wine; the higher you climb, they say, the farther misfortune stays away. That year's Double Ninth on the Si River was climbed quite unlike other years: several thousand children climbing the same mountain, the same stone stair, and what they sought wasn't to escape misfortune, but immortality.

Chending Temple opened its gate once every three years; each time several thousand children came to climb this stair, and those taken numbered no more than a hundred or so. Over three hundred years — about a hundred openings — ten thousand-odd had passed through the gate. Of those ten thousand, some later reached the ninth layer of Qi Refinement, some stopped all their lives at the third or fourth and went down the mountain to be physicians or caravan guards, some died in secret realms and their bodies were never found; of those who truly laid their foundation and crossed that threshold, in three hundred years, count as you might, there were no more than a hundred or so.

It was three days from Mount Meng to the Si River. The first day was mountain road. Xiaoman carried his grandfather's bow, his mother's sewing kit, the empty purse and the empty notebook in his jacket, a token nobody could see hanging at his chest, and didn't say much all the way. His uncle talked all the way. He told of his own climb up Chending Mountain long ago — how the three hundred steps grew one by one into the clouds, how at step one hundred and sixty his two legs turned into someone else's. By the evening rest he'd told it seven times. At the third telling a new part appeared: at step one hundred and twenty he'd seen a snake. By the fifth the snake was thick as an arm. By the seventh it had flicked its tongue at him, he'd glared at it, and it had left. Xiaoman listened and thought: this snake probably grows every year too.

That night the inns at the mountain's foot were long full, even the woodsheds full, the temple verandas lined with sleepers; for ten coppers his uncle got half a straw pallet in someone's cowshed. Besides them the cowshed held a cow, a father and son from Yanzhou, and a thin boy who said nothing. The cow chewed straw all night, the Yanzhou father snored all night, and the thin boy lay with his eyes open staring at the beams all night. He was fourteen or fifteen, thin as a laundry pole, carrying a bundle bigger than himself, bulging with who knew what. Xiaoman tried talking to him — his name, where from — and he said only two words: "The Suns'." Asked more, he said nothing. In the night Xiaoman heard him tossing on the pallet, murmuring something; leaning closer, he heard: "Three steps a breath, three steps a breath…" He'd been by the river that afternoon and heard his uncle's story too.

Just before dawn Xiaoman took a flatbread from his bundle. Four flatbreads, and on the road his uncle's stories had made him hungry for three; there was one left. He broke off half and put it in his mouth, and as he chewed he saw, at the far end of the pallet, the thin boy called Sun awake too, staring at the flatbread in his hand, his throat working.

Xiaoman looked at the half flatbread, and at the boy.

He thought of that night at the bottom of the valley, of the little fox with its tails cut off, of the half egg and half flatbread he'd broken off for it. What he'd thought then was: it's hungry.

He held out the half flatbread in his hand. "Eat. Three hundred steps to climb today."

The boy stared, took it, crammed it into his mouth, chewed fast, and only when he'd finished remembered to say: "…Thanks." Xiaoman waved it off. The boy said, "I'm called Sun Ergou." Xiaoman said, "Shen Xiaoman." Sun Ergou said: "I'll remember."

Below the mountain gate another stretch of ground had been roped off; inside the rope stood a dozen grey-robed stewards, checking each child's age and birthplace, and collecting weapons. Anyone carrying a sword, a blade, a bow or a staff had to take it off and hand it over; a bamboo tally recorded the name, and the thing was hung on a wooden rack. The steward said: "The three trials test the person, not the gear."

So Xiaoman unslung his grandfather's bow. It hung on the rack among a row of gleaming swords and blades, its back wrapped strip by strip in sinew, looking from a distance like a pair of patched trousers among a crowd of new clothes. A boy in a silk gown pointed at it and laughed himself double with his father. Xiaoman paid no attention; he only looked twice at the tally with his name and memorised that the bow hung third row, seventh from the left.

What came was a sedan chair on poles. Four bearers carried it, two servants followed, one holding an umbrella over Ma Xiaobao, one fanning him — neither rain nor sun that day. Ma Xiaobao sat in the chair, another ring fatter than last year, an osmanthus cake in his hand and another in his mouth, cheeks bulging and bulging. Coming from Mount Meng, he'd brought osmanthus cake by the catty — two full food boxes, it was said, and by the Si River he'd eaten one and a half. He spotted Xiaoman at once, swallowed what was in his mouth, and jerked his chin at him. "Well, Shen Xiaoman, you came too? Did your family carry that door home?"

Xiaoman said, "We did, Xiaobao-ge. Put it back a bit crooked."

At the hour of Chen exactly, the bell on the mountain gate struck once — *dang*.

Several thousand children went silent at once. At the top of the stone stair, at some point, an old sweeper had appeared, in a grey cotton jacket, leaning on a bamboo broom, stooped, not so much as glancing down at the thousands below, only sweeping, head down, stroke after stroke, the step under his feet. That step was swept clean already, bright enough to show a reflection, and still he swept. The old disciples at the temple said this old man only ever swept this one step — the three hundredth — and had swept it fifty years. Leaves or snow on other steps, he left alone; only this one. Someone asked him why, and he said: "This step is where a person's first foot lands, coming up." Asked more, he said nothing.

He swept a good while before he spoke, his voice not loud, yet every word dropped clear to the foot of the mountain: "Chending Temple takes people. Not by birth. Not by letters of recommendation —"

A *hum* went through the crowd. Ma Xiaobao's face went white for a moment.

The old man went on: "— by three things only. Legs. Head. Nerve."

**First trial · Legs.**

Three hundred stone steps, one stick of incense.

The moment the old sweeper finished, a steward by the gate lit a stick of incense in a bronze burner and called "Begin." Before the word had landed several thousand children charged up in a mob, raising dust on the stair, pushing and shoving, crying for fathers, crying for mothers, trampling others' shoes and having their own trampled, a proper pot of porridge — for all the world like a flock of ducks with the cage door opened.

label.zh: 走在最后，三步一吸，三步一呼
label.en: At the back: three steps in, three steps out

exits.means: climbs steadily at an even pace, counting breaths, like a hunter on a long trail

story.zh:
沈小满却没有冲。

他走在最后面。他想起舅舅说的那句「我爬到一百六十级，腿就动不了了」——虽说那级数这三天里又长了二十级；又想起他爹说的，蹲一只鹿，越急，鹿越不来；追一头鹿，越急，鹿跑得越远。上山的路，是山的；你跟山抢，山不让你。他便一级一级地走，数着自己的呼吸，三步一吸，三步一呼，那是他在柴垛上练了大半年的吐纳，也是他爹在山里追一头走得很稳的鹿时的步子。

马小宝在一百二十级就坐下了。他本来就不是自己爬上来的，是两个家丁一左一右架着胳膊，半拖半抬弄上来的。那扫地老头站在石阶顶上，远远地朝这边看了一眼，也不说话，就只看了一眼。两个家丁给他看得脖子一缩，乖乖地把马小宝放下了。马小宝坐在一百二十级的台阶上，从怀里摸出一块压扁了的桂花糕，一面吃，一面骂那两个家丁不中用。

走到一百三十级上下，他看见了牛棚里那个兖州来的孩子。那孩子是跟着头一拨冲上去的，这时候扶着崖壁，脸白得像一张纸，一口一口地倒气，两条腿抖得像筛糠。他看见小满，眼睛一亮，像是看见了一根救命的绳子，喊道：「兄弟！拉我一把！」

小满在他身边站了一站。

他是想拉的。可他知道，这一拉，他三步一吸、三步一呼的那口气就断了；气一断，他自己也要在这里坐下。他爹说过，山里遇见别人掉进坑里，先看看自己脚底下站稳了没有；自己都没站稳，伸手去拉，是两个人一起掉进去。

小满便没有伸手。他只道：「别冲了。三步一口气。跟着我的脚。」

那孩子愣了一愣，便跟在他后头，一步一步地走。走了几十级，那孩子的气渐渐喘匀了。又走了几十级，到了两百三十级上下，那孩子终于还是一屁股坐了下去，摆着手道：「兄弟，你走，你走……我不行了。」

走出去十几级，他听见身后那孩子在哭，哭得很小声，像是怕人听见。小满没有回头。他心里有一点难过，又有一点说不出的东西，像是在山里头一回看见他爹把一只受了伤走不动的小鹿，留在了雪地里。他爹那一回说：「山里的事，就是这样。」

小满那时候不懂。这时候他一面走，一面想，好像懂了一点。可他又想：等我哪一天站得够稳了，我要拉。拉得动几个，拉几个。

走到一百五十级的时候，他从一个扎两根小辫子的姑娘身边走过去——不对，是那姑娘从他身边冲过去。她没坐下，也没哭，冲过他身边的时候，他只看见一个鼻头冻得通红的侧脸，像一根萝卜，咬着牙，一口气往上冲，冲得小辫子一甩一甩的。那个背影，瞧着有点眼熟。小满想多看两眼，她已经冲上去了，只剩一截小辫子在雾里一晃，就没了。

他没有想到，那姑娘一直冲到了第三百级，一次也没有坐下。这是后话。

一百六十级到了。

这一级台阶，同别的台阶也没什么两样，一样是青石的，一样给几百年的鞋底磨得中间凹下去一块。只是台阶边上的崖壁上，不知什么年月，给人用石头、用刀、用指甲，刻满了密密麻麻的字，一层压着一层，有的是名字，有的是年月，有的只是一道杠。小满瞧不清都刻的什么，只看出来，刻在这里的，都是在这一级上坐下过的人。

小满的腿，这时候也沉了，沉得像绑了两块磨盘。可他没有停，也没有快，仍是三步一吸，三步一呼。过那一级的时候，他心里说：回去跟舅舅说，就说我走了三百五十级。横竖他那一百六十级，明年怕是要长到两百。

香快烧完的时候，山门底下忽然一阵吹吹打打。

原来是方才那顶滑竿，四个轿夫抬着，又上来了。马小宝坐在滑竿上，手里又换了一块桂花糕，一路颠颠簸簸，颠得桂花糕的渣子落了一身。滑竿一口气抬到了石阶顶上，一个执事迎上去，从马家家丁手里接过一封信，信封上盖着县衙鲜红的大印。那执事看了看，又看了看那扫地的老头，拱了拱手，小声道：「瞿老……荐书。县里的。按例，可补一试。」

扫地的老头没有说话，低下头，接着扫他那一级台阶，扫得很是用力。

滑竿从他身边抬过去的时候，那扫帚不偏不倚，一下扫在前头一个轿夫的脚面上。那轿夫「哎哟」一声，一个趔趄，滑竿登时一歪，马小宝连人带糕从滑竿上滚了下来，骨碌碌滚过最后两级，四仰八叉地躺在了第三百级上。他手里那块桂花糕，一路滚，一路还攥得紧紧的，一口也没掉。

扫地的老头看了一眼，道：「上来了。」便又低头扫地。

走着走着，雾一下子薄了。

他抬起头来，只觉眼前一亮，登时站住了。

雾在他脚底下。一整片的白，平平地铺开去，一直铺到天边，白得像一床新弹的棉被，蒙山、泗水、县城、石坳村，统统给盖在了底下。棉被上头，是明晃晃的太阳，是蓝得发亮的天，是一层一层的殿宇，青瓦，白墙，飞檐一角一角地翘起来，像是一群正要起飞的鸟。风从山顶上吹下来，干干净净的，没有一点烟火气。

他脚底下，只剩最后一级了。那一级，就是扫地老头扫了五十年的那一级，扫得干干净净，一片叶子也没有，青石面上亮得能照见天。先上来的那几百个孩子，一个一个踩上去，踩出一片泥脚印，那老头便跟在后头，一下一下地扫。

小满低头看了看自己的草鞋。那草鞋走了三天的路，爬了两百九十九级台阶，沾满了泥，前头还破了一个洞，一个脚趾头从洞里探出来。他抬起脚，又放下了，想了一想，弯下腰，把草鞋底在上一级台阶的边沿上刮了刮，刮一下，看一看，又刮一下，刮干净了，这才抬脚，轻轻地踩了上去。

扫地的老头正扫到他身边，扫帚停了一停。

香烧完的时候，沈小满站在了第三百级石阶上。

他在心里说道：舅舅，我替你走上来了。

扫地的老头拄着扫帚，第一次抬起眼皮，看了他一眼。

那一眼看的是他的脚，又看他的胸口，看他一起一伏的那口气。小满心里「咯噔」一下，登时想起银月临睡前那个「藏」字来。三步一吸，三步一呼，那是《吐纳经》上的法子，是他在柴垛上一夜一夜练出来的——可这老头看得出来么？

他赶紧张大了嘴，呼哧呼哧地喘起粗气来，喘得跟方才那个拉风箱的孩子一模一样，一面喘，一面拿袖子擦汗，擦得十分卖力。

扫地的老头看了他一会儿，把眼皮垂了下去，又扫地了。
story.en:
Shen Xiaoman didn't charge.

He walked at the very back. He remembered his uncle's "at step one hundred and sixty my legs wouldn't move" — though in three days the number had grown another twenty; and his father's saying: waiting for a deer, the more you hurry, the less it comes; chasing a deer, the more you hurry, the farther it runs. The road up the mountain belongs to the mountain; race the mountain, and it won't let you by. So he walked it step by step, counting his breath, three steps a breath in, three steps a breath out — the breathing he'd practised on the woodpile for the better part of a year, and the pace of his father trailing a deer that walked very steady in the mountains.

Ma Xiaobao sat down at step one hundred and twenty. He hadn't climbed there himself anyway; two servants had half dragged, half carried him up by the arms. The old sweeper at the top looked this way once from far off, said nothing, just looked once. The servants' necks shrank, and they obediently set Ma Xiaobao down. Ma Xiaobao sat on step one hundred and twenty, took a squashed osmanthus cake from his coat, and ate it while cursing the two servants for useless.

Around step one hundred and thirty he saw the Yanzhou boy from the cowshed. The boy had charged up with the first wave, and now clung to the cliff wall, face white as paper, gasping breath after breath, legs shaking like sieves. Seeing Xiaoman, his eyes lit as if at a rope thrown to a drowning man. "Brother! Pull me up!"

Xiaoman stopped beside him for a moment.

He wanted to pull. But he knew that if he did, the breath of three steps in and three out would break; break the breath, and he'd be sitting down here himself. His father had said: when you meet someone fallen into a pit in the mountains, first see if your own feet are steady; if you're not steady yourself and reach out to pull, the two of you fall in together.

So Xiaoman didn't reach out. He said only: "Stop charging. Three steps a breath. Follow my feet."

The boy hesitated, then followed behind him, step by step. After a few dozen steps his breathing evened out. A few dozen more, around step two hundred and thirty, the boy sat down after all, waving his hands. "Brother, you go, you go… I can't."

A dozen steps further up he heard the boy crying behind him, very quietly, as though afraid of being heard. Xiaoman didn't look back. He was a little sad, and there was something else he couldn't name, like the first time in the mountains he'd seen his father leave a wounded fawn that couldn't walk in the snow. His father had said that time: "That's how things are in the mountains."

Xiaoman hadn't understood then. Now, walking, thinking, he seemed to understand a little. But he also thought: the day I'm standing steady enough, I'll pull. As many as I can pull, I'll pull.

At step one hundred and fifty he passed a girl with two little braids — no, it was she who passed him, charging. She didn't sit, didn't cry; charging past him, all he saw was a profile with a nose frozen red, like a radish, teeth gritted, charging up in one breath, braids flicking. That back looked a bit familiar. Xiaoman wanted a second look, but she'd already gone up; only the end of a braid flicked once in the mist, and was gone.

He hadn't imagined that girl would charge all the way to step three hundred without sitting down once. But that is for later.

Step one hundred and sixty.

The step was no different from the others — the same bluestone, worn hollow in the middle by centuries of soles. Only the cliff wall beside it had been carved, in who knew what years, with stones, with knives, with fingernails, crowded with writing, layer on layer — names, dates, sometimes just a stroke. Xiaoman couldn't make out what they said; he could only tell that the ones carved here were all people who had sat down on this step.

By now Xiaoman's legs were heavy too, heavy as if tied to two millstones. But he didn't stop, and didn't speed up; still three steps in, three steps out. Passing that step he said in his heart: back home I'll tell Uncle I walked three hundred and fifty. His one hundred and sixty will probably grow to two hundred by next year.

When the incense was nearly burned out, a din of drums and pipes suddenly broke out at the foot of the mountain gate.

It was that sedan chair again, four bearers, coming up. Ma Xiaobao sat in it with a fresh osmanthus cake, jolting all the way, crumbs all over him. The chair was carried straight up to the top; a steward went to meet it and took a letter from the Ma servants, the envelope stamped with the county yamen's bright red seal. The steward looked at it, then at the old sweeper, cupped his hands and said low: "Elder Qu… a letter of recommendation. From the county. By custom, he may make up the first trial."

The old sweeper said nothing; he lowered his head and went on sweeping his step, very hard.

As the chair passed him the broom, without deviating an inch, swept across the front bearer's foot. The bearer yelped and stumbled, the chair tipped, and Ma Xiaobao, cake and all, tumbled out, rolled over the last two steps, and lay spread-eagled on step three hundred. The osmanthus cake in his hand he'd clutched tight the whole way; not a crumb lost.

The old sweeper glanced at him. "He's up." And swept on.

As he walked the mist suddenly thinned.

He looked up, and his eyes filled with light, and he stood stock still.

The mist was below his feet. One whole sheet of white, spread flat to the edge of the sky, white as a newly fluffed quilt, covering Mount Meng, the Si River, the county town, Shi'ao Village. Above the quilt was a blazing sun, a sky so blue it shone, halls rising tier on tier, blue tiles, white walls, flying eaves curling up one corner after another like a flock of birds about to take wing. The wind blew down from the peak, clean, without a trace of cooking smoke.

Under his feet only the last step remained — the one the old sweeper had swept for fifty years, swept spotless, not a leaf on it, the bluestone bright enough to hold the sky. The several hundred children up first had trodden onto it one by one, leaving muddy prints, and the old man followed behind them, sweeping stroke by stroke.

Xiaoman looked down at his straw sandals. Three days on the road and two hundred and ninety-nine steps had caked them with mud, and a hole in the front let a toe peek through. He lifted his foot, set it down again, thought, bent over, and scraped the sole of his sandal on the edge of the step below — scraped once, looked, scraped again — and when it was clean, lifted his foot and set it gently on the step.

The old sweeper, sweeping beside him just then, paused his broom.

When the incense burned out, Shen Xiaoman stood on the three hundredth step.

He said in his heart: Uncle, I've walked up for you.

The old sweeper leaned on his broom and for the first time raised his eyelids and looked at him.

He looked at his feet, then his chest, the breath rising and falling. Xiaoman's heart gave a jolt, and he remembered Yinyue's "hide" before she slept. Three steps in, three steps out — that was the method from *The Classic of Breathing*, practised night after night on the woodpile — could this old man tell?

He quickly opened his mouth wide and panted, huffing and puffing just like the boy who'd been blowing like a bellows, mopping sweat with his sleeve as he panted, very diligently.

The old sweeper looked at him a while, let his eyelids drop, and swept again.

exits.means: rushes up the steps as fast as possible

story.zh:
小满也冲了。几千只鸭子里，多他一只不多。

冲到一百五十级上下，他的腿忽然沉了——不是累，是像有人往他两条腿上，一边挂了一块磨盘，越急，磨盘越重。身边的孩子一个接一个地坐下去，有的喘，有的哭。

一百六十级。他停下来，扶着膝盖，大口大口地喘气。崖壁上刻满了字，都是在这一级上坐下过的人刻的。二十年前，舅舅在这儿坐了一炷香，看着别人一个一个从他身边走过去。

他想起他爹说的：追一头鹿，越急，鹿跑得越远。他站直了，三步一吸，三步一呼，不快，也不停。

走到一百五十级的时候，他从一个扎两根小辫子的姑娘身边走过去——不对，是那姑娘从他身边冲过去。她没坐下，也没哭，冲过他身边的时候，他只看见一个鼻头冻得通红的侧脸，像一根萝卜，咬着牙，一口气往上冲，冲得小辫子一甩一甩的。那个背影，瞧着有点眼熟。小满想多看两眼，她已经冲上去了，只剩一截小辫子在雾里一晃，就没了。

香只剩一指的时候，他站在了第三百级石阶上，两条腿抖得像两根面条。扫地的老头抬起眼皮，看了他一眼，那一眼的意思大约是：鸭子里头，也有会自己停下来的。
story.en:
Xiaoman charged too. Among several thousand ducks, one more made no difference.

Around step one hundred and fifty his legs suddenly went heavy — not tired: as if someone had hung a millstone on each; the more he hurried, the heavier they got. Around him children sat down one after another, some panting, some crying.

Step one hundred and sixty. He stopped, hands on his knees, gasping. The cliff wall was crowded with carvings — all by people who had sat down on this step. Twenty years ago his uncle had sat here the length of a stick of incense, watching others walk past him one by one.

He remembered his father's saying: chasing a deer, the more you hurry, the farther it runs. He straightened up — three steps in, three steps out; not fast, and not stopping.

At step one hundred and fifty he passed a girl with two little braids — no, it was she who passed him, charging. She didn't sit, didn't cry; charging past him, all he saw was a profile with a nose frozen red, like a radish, teeth gritted, charging up in one breath, braids flicking. That back looked a bit familiar. Xiaoman wanted a second look, but she'd already gone up; only the end of a braid flicked once in the mist, and was gone.

With only a finger's width of incense left, he stood on the three hundredth step, legs shaking like two noodles. The old sweeper raised his eyelids and looked at him once; the look meant, roughly: even among ducks there's one that knows how to stop.
